units: the young deer is born as the cold season ends
at birth it wears a coat covered in pale spots
through its first weeks it lies motionless among the plants
its pale fur makes it hard to tell apart from the ground
its mother moves off to feed and comes back to suckle it
that distance keeps scent away from the hiding place
once its legs grow firm it follows its mother along the tracks
the spots fade when the warmth returns
before the next cold it joins a group of its own kind
text: The cold season loosens its grip, and the fawn arrives in a clearing, too weak to follow its mother beyond a few paces. For its first weeks it lies flat among the tall grass, quite still, and the pale spots across its back blur into the dry leaves. The doe wanders off to graze, then comes back at steady intervals to suckle, so that little scent gathers about the hiding place. When the thin legs firm up at last, the youngster trails after her and learns which tracks can be trusted. Warmth returns; the spots fade and the coat darkens. There follows a season of grazing alone, of choosing tender shoots by instinct. Before the cold comes round again, it falls in with a herd and drifts with them towards the sheltered slopes. The clearing where it all began now means nothing to it at all.

units: the mare had been limping since the day before
the assistant first put the trouble down to a knock
a stone had in fact wedged itself under the animal’s foot
that stone crushed the tissue at every step
without quick action a pocket of pus would have formed
the handler cleaned out the cavity and dressed the wound
the animal was moved onto soft ground that cushions each step
the neglected state of its mane showed poor grooming
the team now checks the feet before every outing
text: The mare had been limping since the previous day, and the stable assistant put it down to a knock against a gatepost. The examination told a different story. A sharp stone had worked its way between the frog and the wall of the hoof, and it crushed the tissue at every step. Left where it lay, that pressure would have driven inflammation deep into the foot and raised an abscess awkward to drain. The handler pared out the cavity, cleaned the wound and bound it under a thick pad held by adhesive tape. Since the animal fretted at being kept still, it was led to a sandy yard whose loose footing cushioned each stride. A matted mane, the mark of neglected grooming, prompted the team to overhaul its routine. The gait ran smooth again within weeks, and the feet are now checked before every outing.

units: a claw left too long ends up wounding the underside of the paw
one should pick a moment when the animal is dozing
the base of the toe is pressed so that the claw comes out
a coloured band marks where the blood vessels run
the cut must stop short of that band
going past that limit brings on bleeding
a tool with a curved blade suits better than an ordinary clipper
it is advisable to break off the session if the animal stiffens
a treat makes the later sessions easier
text: A claw left to grow too long throws off the footing of a cat and will in time curl round and press into the soft pad beneath. The steps set out below deal with the matter without alarming the animal in any way. Choose a settled moment, some while after a meal, when the cat lies dozing across a lap. Take up one paw gently, press the base of the toe so that the claw slides clear of its sheath, and look for the pink band through which the vessels run. The cut must stop well short of that band, or a painful bleed will follow. A tool with a curved blade answers better than an ordinary clipper, whose jaws crush the horn instead of severing it. Should the animal stiffen, break off the session and take it up the next day, one paw at a time. A treat at the end makes the sessions that follow a good deal easier.

units: two neighbouring shelters take in abandoned animals
the first houses every animal in a pen of its own
the second puts compatible animals into small groups
keeping them apart cuts the spread of disease
grouping them lowers the behaviour that comes of boredom
adoptions are settled sooner in the collective setting
quarrels on the other hand break out more often there
both teams keep the same health record
they pass residents to one another as space falls free
text: Two shelters, a valley apart, take in the abandoned animals of the district, yet they work along opposite lines. The first gives every resident a pen of its own, from arrival to departure. A keeper there defends the choice on grounds of contagion: mange travels slowly when muzzles never meet. The second sorts compatible temperaments into small groups, and its director reports a sharp drop in compulsive licking and in the barking that boredom brings. The adoption books bear the difference out. Animals leave sooner from the collective site, where visitors watch them play off one another. Scuffles, though, break out more readily there, and a bitten resident has to be pulled aside at once. Both teams keep the same health record, and each passes animals to the other as soon as a space falls free.

units: the farmyard belongs to an uncle of the narrator
the cockerel has a red growth on top of its head
a hard spike stands out at the back of its legs
the hens roll about in the dry dust
the ducks have a shallow pond to themselves
the geese announce visitors with their cries
a cat sleeps on the woodpile
the uncle hands out the grain before nightfall
text: You ought to see the farmyard my uncle keeps, it is quite a show. The cockerel lords it over the lot of them: that red comb goes up the moment the gate swings, and the hard spur behind each leg makes him worth avoiding. The hens spend the whole afternoon rolling about in the dry dust with their feathers puffed out, and they get up grey from beak to claw. Down the slope a bit, the ducks have a shallow pond they empty and fill again all day long with those flat bills. As for the geese, you hear them well before you see them: let a car turn onto the track and the whole lot start shrieking together. On the woodpile a ginger cat sleeps through the racket without stirring. Then my uncle comes round with his grain bucket before dark, the same hour every evening, and it all goes quiet.

units: the earliest animal collections served to impress visitors
the beasts were shut behind narrow bars
wider cages later imitated the settings they came from
the parks began to breed threatened species
releases into the wild have been attempted
captivity weakens the habits needed for survival
the writer holds that protecting wild places must come first
he grants that some species survive only under human watch
text: The first animal collections existed to dazzle a visitor: a big cat behind narrow bars stood for power, and nobody troubled over the creature wasting away inside them. Wider cages came later, planted with trees and dug out into pools, meant to echo the settings the animals had come from. Then the parks claimed a duty of rescue: breeding scarce species, keeping books of descent, releasing stock born in confinement. That last step deserves a harder look. A predator fed at a fixed hour loses the habits that keep it alive, and its return to the wild fails more often than not. Those budgets would do more good spent on the ground itself, on wooded corridors, on rivers freed of their weirs. Let it be granted, even so, that a handful of species now hangs on under human watch alone.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the trainer grew up on an isolated farm
an accident took the sight of her father
she then trained a dog to guide her father
that success brought other requests
she turned a barn into a training space
she picks puppies for their calm in the face of noise
she refuses rewards founded on fear
her former pupils come back to consult her
text: The trainer spent her childhood on an outlying farm, among plough horses and sheepdogs. When a farm machine took the sight of her father, she set about teaching a young bitch to walk him between the house and the byre. The dog learnt to slow at every step and to lay her muzzle against his hand before any obstacle stood in the way. Word of it travelled, and families began knocking at the farm door for help of the same sort. Short of room, she cleared the barn and laid it out for training, with ramps, slippery boards and swinging doors. She picks her puppies for indifference to clatter rather than for liveliness, since a nervous animal freezes at the worst moment. Having seen what fear produces, she will have nothing to do with harsh correction. Her old pupils still come back to ask her advice.

units: the new tank of a public aquarium is assessed
the curved panes warp the shape of the fish
lighting that was too harsh brought out the glare of the scales
the fish gathered in one corner of the tank
an artificial current was added to spread the fish out
filters have softened the lighting
the visitor route stays too narrow near the entrance
the writer recommends widening that passage
the display is judged a success despite these faults
text: The tank opened in the mild season deserves a hard look before any praise. Its curved panes flatter from a distance, yet they warp the outlines as soon as one steps close: a tail fin reads far broader than it truly is. The lighting, harsh at first, set the scales glittering until the dark markings along the back were lost. The fish, put out by all that glare, packed themselves into a blind corner and went unseen. The staff have since responded on both counts. An artificial current now spreads them through the whole volume, and tinted filters have taken the edge off the beams. One serious fault remains, in the visitor route, so narrow near the entrance that groups jam there and shuffle. Widening the passage is called for. Even with these reservations, the display stands comparison with the best of its kind.

units: the writer writes to a breeder to ask for advice
he is torn between two species to keep at home
the rabbit needs a daily space to run in
the bird copes better with long absences
the rabbit gnaws any cable within reach
the bird keeps up a steady noise that is hard to bear
the writer lives in a cramped flat
he asks for a reply before his planned visit
text: Madam, I hope you will forgive my writing to you, for your years of breeding will guide me better than the leaflets I have read. I am torn between a rabbit and a bird kept for company, and each case seems to me equally sound. The first needs a space to run in every evening, without which its muscles waste away; the second takes my long absences in its stride, which weighs with me, since I am often away from home. Against that, a rabbit gnaws through any cable left within its reach, while a bird keeps up a steady whistling that my neighbours are unlikely to bear kindly for long. My own flat is cramped, and that counts heavily in the balance, with no balcony to extend it. Might I trouble you for an answer before my visit next week? I remain, with every good wish, yours faithfully.

units: the antlers of deer drop and grow again with each yearly cycle
the horns of cattle lengthen without ever falling off
antlers are made of bone
horns sit on a bony core wrapped in a hard sheath
growing antlers again calls for rich feeding
the males use these growths when they fight
the females of certain species carry horns as well
fallen antlers are gnawed by small mammals
text: One question comes up again and again on a country walk: are antlers and horns the same thing? They are not, and the clearest difference lies in what becomes of them. The rack of a stag drops away once the rutting season closes and grows back whole in the cycle that follows, while the horn of an ox lengthens without pause and never parts from the skull. What are they made of? The first is plain bone, fed while it grows by a velvety skin; the second wraps a bony core in a hard fibrous sheath. Does such regrowth cost the animal much? It does, and it calls for feed rich in minerals. What are these growths for? Males measure themselves against rivals with them. Do females go without? Not always: in certain species they carry horns too. And afterwards? Antlers shed on the ground are gnawed away by voles and squirrels.
